overview.title: 📖 Overview: Rabbi Akiva's Questions in the Meat Market
overview.subtitle: Keritot 15a–15b
overview.hebrewSource: שָׁאַלְתִּי אֶת רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל וְאֶת רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בָּאִיטְלֵיס שֶׁל עֵימָאוּם
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens by finishing the discussion of slaughtering a mother animal and its offspring, testing whether 'differentiated names' or 'differentiated bodies' drives multiple liability. It then shifts to one of Shas's most memorable scenes: Rabbi Akiva recalls asking Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua three difficult questions while they shopped for an animal at the meat market of Emmaus, for the wedding feast of Rabban Gamliel's son. None of the three had a received tradition on any question, but each was answered, or challenged, through an a fortiori inference: whether a sister who is simultaneously father's-sister and mother's-sister generates one offering or three; whether an animal's dangling limb transmits impurity like a severed one; and whether slaughtering five offerings outside the Temple in one lapse of awareness creates one sin offering or five. The daf closes with a detailed baraita sorting out exactly how pots, lapses of awareness, and separate animals combine (or don't) to multiply liability.

slides.title: 🐐 Animal and Offspring — Two Theories Behind One Ruling
slides.subtitle: Sumakhos says two sets of lashes for slaughtering a mother and its offspring twice — but why?

steps.content: 1️⃣ Case: one slaughters an animal, then its granddaughter, then finally its daughter — the third slaughter completes TWO 'mother and offspring' violations at once
2️⃣ Sumakhos (in R' Meir's name): liable to eighty lashes — two full sets

3️⃣ Rava's theory: this parallels Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri's mother-in-law ruling — liability multiplies wherever the Torah gives the relationships differentiated names, even without differentiated bodies

4️⃣ Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak's competing theory: it's really about differentiated bodies — three separate animals were slaughtered, unlike the single woman in the mother-in-law case (where Rabbi Yoḥanan b. Nuri's logic wouldn't even apply, since Sumakhos might rest on the verse's 'lewdness' passage treating it as one violation)

callout.label: Open question:
callout.text: The two theories predict different outcomes in edge cases — whether it's the names or the bodies doing the real work of multiplying liability.

slides.title: 🥩 Rabbi Akiva's Three Questions at Emmaus
slides.subtitle: Asked of Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua while shopping for a wedding feast animal
rows: Sister who is also father's-sister and mother's-sister
One sin offering for the whole relationship, or three — one per prohibition name, despite it being a single woman?
A dangling (nearly severed) limb on an animal
Does it impart ritual impurity like a fully severed limb, or not, since it's still technically attached?
Slaughtering five offerings outside the Temple in one lapse
One sin offering for the whole spree, or five — one per animal?

callout.label: The teachers' honest answer each time:
callout.text: 'We have not heard a tradition on this' — followed by an attempt to resolve it through a fortiori reasoning from a related, transmitted halakha.

slides.title: 🦵 The Dangling Limb — A Passover Surgery Story
slides.subtitle: Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua answer from a real medical practice in Jerusalem

lines.speaker: R' Akiva
lines.text: What is the status of an animal's dangling limb — does it transmit impurity?

lines.speaker: Teachers
lines.text: We have no tradition on animals — but we know about people: a dangling human limb is pure. Here's how we know.

lines.speaker: The account
lines.text: People afflicted with boils in Jerusalem would visit a doctor on Passover eve, who would cut the diseased limb down to a hairbreadth of flesh, then impale it on a thorn so the patient could pull it fully off himself — without either doctor or patient becoming impure by contact with a severed limb.

lines.speaker: Conclusion
lines.text: Both the patient and the doctor then brought their Paschal offerings in purity — proof the dangling limb, while still attached, imparted no impurity.

lines.speaker: R' Akiva's inference
lines.text: A fortiori: if a human limb (whose severed-limb impurity is severe) causes no impurity while dangling, surely an animal's limb (whose severed-limb impurity is more lenient) causes none either.

callout.label: Gemara's footnote:
callout.text: The rule works only when the limb is torn off with one forceful pull — gradual separation (as with squeezed-out liquid) may render it 'detached' earlier.

slides.title: 🔪 Slaughtering Five Offerings Outside — Kal Vaḥomer and Its Rebuttal
slides.subtitle: The most contested of Rabbi Akiva's three questions

nodes.content: ❓ Slaughtering 5 offerings outside the Temple in one lapse: 1 sin offering, or 5?

💡 Rabbi Yehoshua's a fortiori: one who eats meat from a SINGLE offering cooked in five separate pots owes five guilt offerings for misuse (me'ila) — surely slaughtering five separate ANIMALS is at least as severe!

🛑 Rabbi Akiva's rebuttal: me'ila carries unique stringencies — it treats 'feeding another' like eating, 'benefiting another' like personal benefit, and even lets separate small benefits over time combine. None of these apply to ordinary sin offerings, so the inference doesn't transfer

🔄 Rabbi Shimon later clarifies: the real question Rabbi Akiva asked wasn't about slaughtering at all — it was about eating notar (leftover offering meat) from five separate offerings, a closer parallel to Rabbi Yehoshua's five-pots case

callout.label: Unresolved:
callout.text: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yehoshua ever accepted Rabbi Akiva's rebuttal — and finds the answer only by checking how later baraitot actually ruled.

slides.title: 📊 How Many Offerings? The Resolving Baraita
slides.subtitle: A later baraita finally settles how pots, lapses, and separate animals combine

boxes.title: One offering, one lapse
items: 5 pieces of notar from ONE offering, cooked in 5 pots, eaten in ONE lapse → just 1 sin offering
Same offering, but eaten across 5 separate lapses → 5 sin offerings, since awareness divides liability

boxes.title: Five offerings, one lapse
items: 5 pieces of notar from 5 SEPARATE offerings, eaten in one lapse → 5 sin offerings (differentiated bodies), per the first tanna
Rabbi Yosei b. Rabbi Yehuda dissents: even this case yields only 1 sin offering, since it's still one repeated transgression in one lapse

callout.label: Contrast with me'ila:
callout.text: Eating from 5 pots of a single offering BEFORE its blood is sprinkled (still fully consecrated) yields 5 separate guilt offerings for misuse, even in one lapse — confirming misuse really does follow different, more stringent rules than ordinary sin offerings.

summary.principle: Whether one bite, one act, or one lapse of awareness generates a single offering or many depends on precise technical factors — differentiated names, differentiated bodies, separate lapses of awareness, and whether the transgression is an ordinary sin offering or the uniquely stringent case of misusing consecrated property.

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: the Sages' most difficult unresolved dilemmas are worked out through careful a fortiori reasoning, tested rigorously for hidden differences between the cases compared

quiz.q: At what event does Rabbi Akiva recall asking his three unresolved questions to Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua?
o: A funeral
A meat market in Emmaus, while shopping for an animal for Rabban Gamliel's son's wedding feast
A Sanhedrin session
A Yom Kippur service
quiz.e: Rabbi Akiva recalls asking these questions at the meat market (itlis) of Emmaus, where the group had gone to purchase an animal for the wedding feast of Rabban Gamliel's son.

quiz.q: How do Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua resolve Rabbi Akiva's question about whether an animal's dangling limb transmits ritual impurity?
o: By citing an explicit verse
By analogy to a documented medical practice in Jerusalem, where a dangling human limb was shown to cause no impurity
By majority vote
They declare the question unanswerable
quiz.e: They cite the practice of people afflicted with boils who had their nearly-severed limbs removed by a doctor on Passover eve without either party becoming impure, proving a dangling limb causes no impurity — and infer the same for animals a fortiori.

quiz.q: What rebuttal does Rabbi Akiva offer to Rabbi Yehoshua's a fortiori inference from misuse of consecrated property (me'ila) to slaughtering five offerings outside the Temple?
o: That me'ila does not actually require multiple offerings
That me'ila carries unique stringencies (treating feeding others like eating, and combining benefits over time) that don't apply to ordinary sin offerings
That slaughtering offerings outside the Temple carries no penalty at all
That Rabbi Yehoshua's testimony was unreliable
quiz.e: Rabbi Akiva argues that misuse of consecrated property has special stringencies not found in ordinary transgressions, so an inference from its rules to ordinary sin-offering liability is invalid.

quiz.q: According to the resolving baraita, how many sin offerings does one owe for eating notar from ONE offering, cooked in five different pots, all within a single lapse of awareness?
o: Five
One
Zero
Ten
quiz.e: The baraita rules that eating notar from a single offering, even prepared in five separate pots, within one lapse of awareness, results in only one sin offering, since it remains one 'body' (one offering).

quiz.q: According to the first tanna in the baraita, how many sin offerings does one owe for eating notar from FIVE separate offerings within a single lapse of awareness — and how does Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, disagree?
o: The first tanna says one; Rabbi Yosei says five
The first tanna says five, since the offerings are differentiated bodies; Rabbi Yosei says only one, since it is still one lapse of awareness
Both agree on one offering total
Both agree on five separate offerings
quiz.e: The first tanna holds that five separate offerings (differentiated bodies) generate five sin offerings even within one lapse; Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, dissents, holding that even eating from five separate offerings within one lapse of awareness yields only one sin offering.
